questions.question: Q1. For the 5″ airframe (J = 0.003 kg·m<sup>2</sup>) with K<sub>p</sub> = 0.6 N·m/rad, what is the closed-loop natural frequency ω<sub>n</sub> = √(K<sub>p</sub>/J)?

explanations.a: Incorrect — that is K<sub>p</sub>/J before the square root divided wrongly.
explanations.c: Incorrect — 200 is K<sub>p</sub>/J; you must take its square root.

questions.question: Q2. With K<sub>d</sub> fixed at 0.04, sweeping K<sub>p</sub> from 0.2 to 1.0 in the simulator makes the overshoot do what?

answers.c: Increase from about 1% to about 29%, crossing the 25% limit near K<sub>p</sub> = 0.8

explanations.a: Incorrect — overshoot changes strongly with K<sub>p</sub>.
explanations.b: Incorrect — the trend is the opposite direction.
explanations.c: Correct — higher K<sub>p</sub> lowers the damping ratio, so overshoot rises (1.18 / 10.85 / 18.65 / 24.54 / 29.16%) and passes the 25% comfort limit around K<sub>p</sub> = 0.8.
explanations.d: Incorrect — the loop stays stable; overshoot rises gradually, not to 100%.

questions.question: Q3. In the K<sub>p</sub> sweep the 2% settling time stays pinned at about 0.60 s. Why is it independent of K<sub>p</sub>?

answers.a: Because the simulator caps it at 0.60 s
answers.b: Because the decay rate ζω<sub>n</sub> = K<sub>d</sub>/(2J) depends only on K<sub>d</sub> and J, not on K<sub>p</sub>
answers.c: Because settling time never depends on any gain
answers.d: Because K<sub>p</sub> and K<sub>d</sub> were both changed together

explanations.a: Incorrect — it is a genuine result of the math, not an artificial cap.
explanations.b: Correct — ζω<sub>n</sub> = K<sub>d</sub>/(2J) = 0.04/(2×0.003) = 6.67 s<sup>−1</sup>, so t<sub>s</sub> = 4/6.67 = 0.60 s regardless of K<sub>p</sub>.
explanations.c: Incorrect — settling time does depend on K<sub>d</sub> and J.
explanations.d: Incorrect — only K<sub>p</sub> was swept; K<sub>d</sub> was held fixed.

questions.question: Q4. With the disturbance torque enabled (τ<sub>d</sub> = 0.0175 N·m) and pure PD control, the steady-state tilt at K<sub>p</sub> = 0.6 is about 1.67°. What removes it entirely?

explanations.a: Incorrect — derivative gain affects the transient, not the steady-state offset.
explanations.b: Incorrect — lowering K<sub>p</sub> makes the droop larger (e<sub>ss</sub> = τ<sub>d</sub>/K<sub>p</sub>).
explanations.c: Correct — the integral term accumulates the residual error and generates the exact counter-torque, driving the steady-state error to zero.
explanations.d: Incorrect — integral action removes it completely.

questions.question: Q5. Why does the Ziegler–Nichols method require the rate-loop lag model rather than the ideal 1/(J s<sup>2</sup>) plant?

answers.a: Because the ideal plant is too simple to simulate
answers.b: Because a pure double integrator oscillates at every proportional gain, so its ultimate gain is undefined
answers.c: Because the lag model is more accurate at high thrust
answers.d: Because Ziegler–Nichols only works on first-order systems

explanations.a: Incorrect — simulability is not the issue.
explanations.b: Correct — with poles on the imaginary axis at all gains, 1/(Js<sup>2</sup>) has no finite stability boundary; the actuator and sensor lags create the finite K<sub>u</sub> the method needs.
explanations.c: Incorrect — it is about the stability boundary existing at all, not thrust accuracy.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Z-N applies to higher-order systems; it needs at least third order for a finite K<sub>u</sub>.

questions.question: Q6. The auto-tune finds K<sub>u</sub> = 19.25 and P<sub>u</sub> = 0.051 s. What is the classic Ziegler–Nichols proportional gain (K<sub>p</sub> = 0.6 K<sub>u</sub>)?

explanations.a: Incorrect — 0.6 is the multiplier, not the result.
explanations.c: Incorrect — 19.25 is K<sub>u</sub> itself; the classic table uses 60% of it.
explanations.d: Incorrect — that would be K<sub>u</sub>/0.6, the wrong direction.

questions.question: Q7. In the simulation, the classic Ziegler–Nichols gains produce roughly 68% overshoot. What does switching to the Tyreus–Luyben table achieve?

answers.b: It raises the integral time (lowers K<sub>i</sub>) and lowers K<sub>p</sub>, dropping overshoot to about 15% while keeping zero steady-state error
answers.c: It removes the integral term entirely
answers.d: It doubles the overshoot for faster response

explanations.a: Incorrect — Tyreus–Luyben is specifically a more robust, stable tuning.
explanations.b: Correct — it backs off the aggressive integral gain (450 → 77) and lowers K<sub>p</sub>, taming overshoot to ~15% (under the 25% target) with e<sub>ss</sub> still zero.
explanations.c: Incorrect — it keeps integral action, just gentler.
explanations.d: Incorrect — it reduces overshoot, not increases it.

questions.question: Q8. In the complementary filter, how does increasing the blend coefficient α (toward 1) change the estimate?

answers.a: It trusts the accelerometer more — less drift, more noise
answers.b: It trusts the gyro more — more drift, less accelerometer noise
answers.c: It has no effect on drift or noise
answers.d: It always reduces both drift and noise

explanations.a: Incorrect — that is the effect of a lower α.
explanations.b: Correct — a higher α lengthens the time constant τ<sub>f</sub> = αΔt/(1−α), trusting the integrated gyro longer (more drift) while filtering more accelerometer noise.
explanations.c: Incorrect — α directly trades drift against noise.
explanations.d: Incorrect — there is a trade-off; you cannot reduce both arbitrarily by moving α one way.

questions.question: Q9. For the reference IMU (bias 0.6°/s, accel noise 1.8°, 400 Hz), which α minimises the combined drift + noise error?

explanations.a: Incorrect — at 0.90 the accelerometer noise dominates (total ~0.43°).
explanations.b: Incorrect — 0.95 is better but not the minimum (total ~0.32°).
explanations.c: Correct — α = 0.98 gives the smallest total error (~0.25°), balancing 0.074° drift against 0.181° noise.
explanations.d: Incorrect — at 0.99 drift grows and the total rises again (~0.28°).

questions.question: Q10. Setting α = 1.0 (pure gyro integration) with a 0.6°/s bias produces what attitude error after 30 s?

explanations.a: Incorrect — the uncorrected bias guarantees error.
explanations.b: Incorrect — 0.25° is the fused result at the optimal α, not pure gyro.
explanations.c: Correct — with no accelerometer correction the bias integrates unbounded: 0.6°/s × 30 s = 18°, and it keeps growing.
explanations.d: Incorrect — drift is monotonic, not oscillatory.
